$comment: The closed vocabulary of the cuisine domain. Each ingredient and method gives its origin: the first year with a firm record of its use as food or in the kitchen, and the place. arrival gives the first firm record in a European kitchen for an item that began elsewhere. circa = true marks an estimate.

branches.name: Haute and restaurant kitchen
branches.scope: The kitchens of courts, grand hotels and restaurants, where chefs set the rules that others copy.

branches.name: Codified home traditions
branches.scope: The cooking of a region or a nation as a named author wrote it down for the home cook.

branches.name: Pastry and confectionery
branches.scope: Sweet work: cakes, tarts, sugar, chocolate and the plated dessert.

branches.name: Bread
branches.scope: The bakery: leavened and flat bread, sour dough and the oven.

branches.name: Preservation and fermentation
branches.scope: Food kept by salt, smoke, acid, drying and microbes: charcuterie, cured fish, pickles and ferments.

branches.name: Street and fast food
branches.scope: Food sold ready to eat at a stall, a cart, a counter or a drive-in.

branches.name: Diet and belief kitchens
branches.scope: Kitchens that a faith or a theory of health rules: what may be eaten, and how.

branches.name: Drink and bar
branches.scope: The cocktail bar, the coffee house and the tea ceremony.

ingredients.name: Wheat
ingredients.note: Einkorn and emmer were sown in the Near East; bread wheat followed. Flour is the base of bread, pastry, roux and pasta.

ingredients.name: Rye
ingredients.note: A hardy grain of the cold north; the dark sour bread of Scandinavia, Germany and Russia.

ingredients.name: Rice
ingredients.note: Asian rice reached Spain with the Moors; paella and risotto came later. Short grain for sushi and risotto.

ingredients.name: Maize
ingredients.note: Domesticated from teosinte; nixtamalised with lime for masa. Columbus took it to Spain.

ingredients.name: Quinoa
ingredients.note: The seed of the Andean highlands; it reached European shops only in the late twentieth century.

ingredients.name: Potato
ingredients.note: Thousands of Andean kinds; Parmentier made it French food after 1772. Pommes purée, frites and chuño.

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.note: Mattioli recorded the pomi d'oro in 1544; the first Italian tomato sauce recipe is of 1692.

ingredients.name: Chilli pepper
ingredients.note: Capsicum went from the Americas round the world in fifty years: to Hungary, India, Sichuan and Korea.

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.note: The base of most savoury cooking, sweated, browned or raw.

ingredients.name: Garlic
ingredients.note: Used raw, confit or roasted; the mark of Provençal and southern cooking.

ingredients.name: Shallot
ingredients.note: A mild onion of the French sauce: beurre blanc, béarnaise and bordelaise start with it.

ingredients.name: Carrot
ingredients.note: Purple and yellow at first; the orange carrot was bred in the Netherlands in the seventeenth century.

ingredients.name: Cabbage
ingredients.note: Kale, cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli are one species, bred in Europe.

ingredients.name: Asparagus
ingredients.note: Cato described its culture; white asparagus is grown in the dark under earth.

ingredients.name: Artichoke
ingredients.note: Bred from the cardoon in Sicily and Naples; Catherine de' Medici took it to France.

ingredients.name: Leek
ingredients.note: A soft onion for soups and vichyssoise; the white is the part used.

ingredients.name: Root vegetables
ingredients.note: Turnip, swede, celeriac, beetroot and parsnip: the winter store of the north.

ingredients.name: Young greens and shoots
ingredients.note: Pea shoots, young leaves, wild garlic and small salad leaves picked young.

ingredients.name: Wild plants and flowers
ingredients.note: Foraged leaves, flowers, berries, moss and needles; the base of the foraging kitchen.

ingredients.name: Truffle
ingredients.note: The black truffle of Périgord and the white truffle of Alba; shaved raw or cooked in sauce.

ingredients.name: Wild mushrooms
ingredients.note: Ceps, morels, chanterelles; dried or fresh, foraged in the autumn and the spring.

ingredients.name: Kombu
ingredients.note: Kelp dried in the sun; with katsuobushi it makes dashi, the base stock of Japan. Rich in glutamate.

ingredients.name: Lemon
ingredients.note: The Arabs grew lemons in Sicily and Spain; the acid of fish dishes and sauces.

ingredients.name: Lime
ingredients.note: The Spanish took limes to the Americas, where they cure ceviche.

ingredients.name: Bitter orange
ingredients.note: The orange of duck à l'orange and marmalade; the sweet orange came later, after 1500.

ingredients.name: Grape
ingredients.note: Eaten fresh, dried, pressed for verjuice or made into wine.

ingredients.name: Verjuice
ingredients.note: The sour juice of unripe grapes; the acid of the medieval sauce before lemon and vinegar.

ingredients.name: Orchard fruit
ingredients.note: Apple, pear, quince, plum and cherry from orchards.

ingredients.name: Peach
ingredients.note: The Romans called it the Persian apple; pêche Melba of 1893 used it.

ingredients.name: Tropical fruit
ingredients.note: Pineapple, mango, passion fruit and papaya; Europe grew pineapples in hothouses from the 1700s.

ingredients.name: Berries
ingredients.note: Lingonberry, cloudberry, sea buckthorn, bilberry, raspberry and strawberry, wild or grown.

ingredients.name: Yuzu
ingredients.note: A sour aromatic citrus of Japan; French chefs took it up in the 1990s.

ingredients.name: Black pepper
ingredients.note: The most traded spice of the ancient world; Rome bought it by the tonne.

ingredients.name: Cinnamon
ingredients.note: Bark of the cinnamon tree; the base of the medieval cameline sauce.

ingredients.name: Clove
ingredients.note: Dried flower buds from the Spice Islands; studs the onion of a classic stock.

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.note: A rhizome used dried in medieval Europe and fresh in Asia.

ingredients.name: Nutmeg and mace
ingredients.note: Seed and aril of one tree; in béchamel and the medieval spice mix.

ingredients.name: Grains of paradise
ingredients.note: A peppery seed from the Guinea coast; a medieval spice that nearly left the kitchen.

ingredients.name: Saffron
ingredients.note: Stigmas of the crocus; it coloured medieval dishes gold. Used now in risotto and bouillabaisse.

ingredients.name: Vanilla
ingredients.note: Totonac people cured the pod of an orchid; the hand pollination of 1841 by Edmond Albius made it a crop.

ingredients.name: Cocoa
ingredients.note: Ground cacao beans drunk with chilli; Europe added sugar.

ingredients.name: Fines herbes
ingredients.note: Parsley, chervil, chives and tarragon, chopped fine; the herb mix of the French kitchen.

ingredients.name: Tarragon
ingredients.note: The herb of béarnaise sauce and of poulet à l'estragon.

ingredients.name: Thyme and bay
ingredients.note: With parsley, the bouquet garni of stocks and braises.

ingredients.name: Coriander leaf
ingredients.note: The leaf herb of Asian and Latin American cooking; the seed is a separate spice.

ingredients.name: Cane sugar
ingredients.note: Crystal sugar reached Europe through the crusades; a costly spice until the plantations.

ingredients.name: Honey
ingredients.note: The sweetener of Europe before sugar.

ingredients.name: Butter
ingredients.note: The fat of the northern French kitchen; it took the place of oil and lard in sauces after 1650.

ingredients.name: Cream
ingredients.note: Double cream and crème fraîche thicken and enrich the sauces of the classic kitchen.

ingredients.name: Cheese
ingredients.note: Strainers with milk fat from about 5500 BC; Parmigiano, Comté and Gruyère are hard cheeses for cooking.

ingredients.name: Hen egg
ingredients.note: Binds, raises, thickens and emulsifies: the tool of mayonnaise, hollandaise, soufflé and custard.

ingredients.name: Beef
ingredients.note: The fillet, the rib and the braising cuts; tournedos Rossini and boeuf bourguignon.

ingredients.name: Veal
ingredients.note: The meat of the calf and the bones of the white and brown stock.

ingredients.name: Lamb
ingredients.note: Saddle, rack and leg; the roast of spring.

ingredients.name: Pork
ingredients.note: Fresh, salted and cured; lard is its fat.

ingredients.name: Foie gras
ingredients.note: Fattened goose or duck liver; a mark of the French luxury kitchen since the eighteenth century.

ingredients.name: Duck
ingredients.note: Breast cooked pink and legs as confit; Peking duck in China.

ingredients.name: Chicken
ingredients.note: The capon and the Bresse chicken of the French kitchen.

ingredients.name: Game birds
ingredients.note: Pheasant, partridge, woodcock and pigeon; the medieval feast added swan, heron and peacock.

ingredients.name: Venison
ingredients.note: Red deer, roe deer and reindeer; hung, roasted and served with a sharp berry sauce.

ingredients.name: Sole and flat fish
ingredients.note: Dover sole, turbot and brill: the fish of the classic kitchen, poached, grilled or meunière.

ingredients.name: Salmon
ingredients.note: Wild in rivers, then farmed after 1970; cured, smoked or cooked pink.

ingredients.name: Cod
ingredients.note: Dried as stockfish and salted as klippfisk; traded from Lofoten through the Middle Ages.

ingredients.name: Tuna
ingredients.note: Raw as sushi in Japan after the 1840s; the fat belly is toro.

ingredients.name: Shellfish
ingredients.note: Lobster, langoustine, crab, scallop and prawn; the luxury of the coast.

ingredients.name: Oyster
ingredients.note: Sergius Orata farmed oysters at Baiae; eaten raw or poached.

ingredients.name: Caviar
ingredients.note: Salted sturgeon roe; a luxury of the Russian court and the French restaurant.

ingredients.name: Sea urchin
ingredients.note: Raw gonads, sweet and briny; uni in Japan.

ingredients.name: Olive oil
ingredients.note: The fat of the south: raw, for frying and for confit.

ingredients.name: Lard
ingredients.note: Rendered pork fat; the frying fat of medieval and peasant kitchens.

ingredients.name: Soy sauce
ingredients.note: Fermented soy beans and wheat. The Dutch East India Company shipped it from Nagasaki from 1647, and to Europe in the 1660s.

ingredients.name: Miso
ingredients.note: Soy paste fermented with koji; in soup, glazes and marinades.

ingredients.name: Vinegar
ingredients.note: Wine or cider made sour by acetic bacteria; the sauce acid of the North.

ingredients.name: Dashi
ingredients.note: Stock of kombu and katsuobushi; its umami taught French chefs a lighter base.

ingredients.name: Wine
ingredients.note: For deglazing, braising and sauce reduction.

ingredients.name: Tofu
ingredients.note: Curd of soy milk pressed into blocks; the protein of the Buddhist kitchen.

ingredients.name: Pulses
ingredients.note: Lentil, chickpea, bean and pea: the protein of the plant kitchen.

ingredients.name: Nuts and seeds
ingredients.note: Almond, hazelnut, walnut, sesame and pumpkin seed; the almond milk of medieval Lent.

ingredients.name: Bread
ingredients.note: Flat bread from about 14,000 years ago; the medieval kitchen thickened sauces with it and served food on trenchers.

ingredients.name: Sodium alginate
ingredients.note: A salt from brown seaweed that sets in contact with calcium: the gel skin of spherification.

ingredients.name: Agar
ingredients.note: A seaweed gel that sets firm and stays firm when warm; it allows a hot jelly.

ingredients.name: Xanthan gum
ingredients.note: A gum made by bacteria; a little thickens a sauce or holds a foam without heat.

ingredients.name: Liquid nitrogen
ingredients.note: Nitrogen at minus 196 °C; it freezes ice cream in seconds and makes powders of fat.

ingredients.name: Lecithin
ingredients.note: An emulsifier from egg yolk or soy; it holds the light airs of the modernist kitchen.

methods.name: Spit roasting
methods.note: Meat turned on a spit before an open fire; the roast of the medieval hall and the rôtisseur.

methods.name: Grilling
methods.note: Food cooked over glowing coals or a hot iron, with char lines.

methods.name: Wood-fire cooking
methods.note: Cooking in embers, ash and smoke; the open fire of the terroir kitchen.

methods.name: Oven roasting
methods.note: Roasting in a closed iron range; the range of the 1800s replaced the open hearth.

methods.name: Braising
methods.note: Meat browned and cooked slowly in a little liquid under a lid.

methods.name: Poaching
methods.note: Cooking in liquid just under the boil: fish in court-bouillon, eggs, fruit.

methods.name: Steaming
methods.note: Cooking in steam over boiling water; the light method of China and of cuisine minceur.

methods.name: Boiling
methods.note: Cooking in boiling liquid; pottery of about 20,000 years ago shows it.

methods.name: Sautéing
methods.note: Quick cooking in a little fat in a wide pan, with the pan moved by the cook.

methods.name: Deep frying
methods.note: Food dropped into hot fat; tempura reached Japan from the Portuguese in the 1500s.

methods.name: Confit
methods.note: Meat cooked slowly in its own fat and kept under it.

methods.name: Stock (fond)
methods.note: Bones, vegetables and herbs simmered for hours; the fonds of the French kitchen.

methods.name: Roux
methods.note: Flour cooked in fat; it thickens sauces and replaced bread as the thickener.

methods.name: Mother sauces
methods.note: A system of base sauces from which each other sauce comes; Escoffier fixed the five in 1903.

methods.name: Emulsion sauce
methods.note: Butter or oil held in egg yolk or a reduction: hollandaise, béarnaise, mayonnaise, beurre blanc.

methods.name: Reduction
methods.note: A liquid boiled down to concentrate its taste and to thicken it, without flour.

methods.name: Bread thickening
methods.note: Sauces of the medieval court thickened with soaked bread, ground almonds or liver.

methods.name: Larding
methods.note: Strips of fat threaded through lean meat with a needle before it is roasted.

methods.name: Aspic and chaud-froid
methods.note: Meat or fish set in a clear jelly of stock; the cold buffet of the grand kitchen.

methods.name: Pâté en croûte
methods.note: Meat baked in a pastry case; the pie of the medieval and classic feast.

methods.name: Knife work
methods.note: Exact cuts: julienne, brunoise, tournée and chiffonade; in Japan the work of the itamae.

methods.name: Plating in the kitchen
methods.note: The chef arranges each plate in the kitchen and the waiter only carries it; nouvelle cuisine made this the norm.

methods.name: Sous vide
methods.note: Food sealed in plastic and cooked in water at an exact low temperature; first for foie gras.

methods.name: Spherification

origin.by: Ferran Adrià and the elBulli team

methods.note: A liquid set in a skin of alginate gel in a calcium bath; it bursts in the mouth.

methods.name: Siphon foam
methods.note: A purée or a liquid aerated with nitrous oxide in a cream siphon: the espuma.

methods.name: Liquid nitrogen freezing
methods.note: Instant freezing at minus 196 °C. In 1901 Marshall proposed liquid air for ice cream at the table; modernist chefs used liquid nitrogen after 1990.

methods.name: Dehydrating
methods.note: Water taken out with dry air or low heat; leathers, crisps and powders.

methods.name: Smoking
methods.note: Food exposed to the smoke of wood or hay; cold smoke cures, hot smoke cooks.

methods.name: Salt curing
methods.note: Salt draws water out of fish and meat: gravlaks, ham, salt cod.

methods.name: Pickling
methods.note: Food kept in vinegar or brine.

methods.name: Lacto-fermentation
methods.note: Lactic bacteria sour vegetables in salt: sauerkraut, kimchi, fermented juices.

methods.name: Koji fermentation
methods.note: The mould Aspergillus oryzae grown on rice or barley makes miso, soy sauce and sake; the Nordic kitchen took it up after 2010.

methods.name: Acid curing
methods.note: Raw fish turned firm and opaque by lime juice in minutes: the cure of ceviche.

methods.name: Raw slicing
methods.note: Raw fish and meat cut to show their grain: sashimi, carpaccio, crudo. The word sashimi is first written in a diary of 1399.

methods.name: Wok cooking
methods.note: Stir-frying in a thin iron pan over high flame, for wok hei, the breath of the wok.
